title: When the Room Burns
premise: Marguerite Joubert, a pest controller with a reputation for taking jobs no one else will, is hired to clear an old farmhouse outside Saint-Aubin where something leaves human fingerprints in the flour and ash. The house's mirrors begin lagging one second behind reality, showing rooms that were, and then showing Marguerite things she never did. Digging into the house's history, she learns that in 1974 the family who lived there drowned their youngest son in the cistern to hide what he'd seen of them — and the thing with fingerprints is his unfinished self, wearing borrowed faces. To survive the frost that is slowly writing itself across every window, Marguerite must return the boy's body to the light he was denied, even as her own reflection starts insisting it was there in 1974 too. In the end she gives the house what it wants instead of herself: the truth spoken aloud by the last living member of the family, freeing the boy but leaving Marguerite unable to trust any mirror again.
about_author: Rafael Marchetti is the pen name of a former building inspector from Lyon who spent a decade cataloguing condemned houses before turning to horror fiction. Their work draws on France's abandoned rural architecture and the quiet violence of family secrets.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Flour
chapters.summary: Marguerite arrives at the Delaunay farmhouse after three prior exterminators quit; she finds small handprints pressed into a flour bin, five-fingered and warm. POV: Marguerite. Beat: professional skepticism curdling into unease.

chapters.title: The Counting Ritual
chapters.summary: She establishes her routines — lights on, doors counted twice nightly — and interviews the sole surviving neighbor, old Madame Perrin, who warns her not to answer anything that knocks at 3 a.m. POV: Marguerite. Beat: false comfort of control.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: The hallway mirror reflects Marguerite raising her cup a full second after she does. She tests every reflective surface in the house; only the mirrors lag, and each night the delay grows. POV: Marguerite. Beat: dread replacing doubt.

chapters.title: What the Mirror Shows
chapters.summary: The mirror displays the kitchen as it looked decades ago — a woman scrubbing a floor that isn't dirty. When Marguerite reaches toward the glass, the reflected room reaches back first. POV: Marguerite. Beat: the boundary between observation and invitation collapses.

chapters.title: Pulled Through
chapters.summary: Sleepless, Marguerite stands too close; the mirror surface gives like cold water and deposits her in the 1974 kitchen, intact but smelling of woodsmoke. She escapes through the pantry door into her present hallway. POV: Marguerite. Beat: terror and a terrible curiosity born together.

chapters.title: The Boy in the Cistern
chapters.summary: Researching the Delaunays, Marguerite learns the youngest son, Étienne, vanished in winter 1974; records list him as 'sent away.' Madame Perrin lets slip that the well was sealed that same week. POV: Marguerite. Beat: grief for a stranger.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't Counted
chapters.summary: A door appears overnight between the bathroom and a wall that should be solid. Her count now comes up thirteen. Inside is a child's bedroom preserved mid-play, toys arranged facing the door. POV: Marguerite. Beat: the house is rearranging itself around her.

chapters.title: Étienne
chapters.summary: In the mirrored world she meets a boy of about eight who calls her by name and asks if she's come to take him out this time. He has flour on his hands. POV: Marguerite. Beat: tenderness entangled with horror.

chapters.title: The Family Album
chapters.summary: Photographs from 1974 show the parents' faces subtly wrong — eyes slightly misplaced, smiles too wide — while Étienne alone looks frightened. The final photo shows all four children; the eldest, Camille, is still alive somewhere. POV: Marguerite. Beat: justice begins to take shape as a debt.

chapters.title: Camille Delaunay
chapters.summary: Marguerite tracks Camille, now seventy and living under another name in Tours, who refuses to speak until Marguerite describes the fingerprints. Then she weeps. POV: split — Marguerite's visit intercut with Camille's memory. Beat: guilt surfacing after fifty years.

chapters.title: What They Did
chapters.summary: Camille confesses: Étienne saw the parents doing something unspeakable in the cellar, and drowning him in the cistern was the family's solution. The body was never moved. POV: Camille's confession framed by Marguerite's silence. Beat: horror revealed as ordinary cowardice.

chapters.title: The Frost Begins
chapters.summary: Back at the house, frost ferns bloom across windows in patterns resembling hands. The heating fails. Each morning the ice covers more glass, and Marguerite realizes the pattern is counting down. POV: Marguerite. Beat: time pressure made visible.

chapters.title: My Reflection's Alibi
chapters.summary: Her mirror-self begins acting independently — mouthing words, pointing toward the cellar. When Marguerite finally reads its lips, the message is: 'You were here.' A 1974 photograph surfaces with a young woman who could be her grandmother. POV: Marguerite. Beat: identity destabilized; is she witness, descendant, or accomplice?

chapters.title: Grandmother's Letters
chapters.summary: In her late grandmother's effects, Marguerite finds letters from Odile Joubert, the Delaunay housekeeper in 1974, describing 'the crying under the floor' and her own silence. Marguerite's inheritance is complicity. POV: Marguerite. Beat: love against duty — her loyalty to family memory versus the boy's claim.

chapters.title: Thirteen Doors
chapters.summary: The house now generates doors faster than she can count them; behind several are moments from 1974 replaying. She witnesses the drowning from inside the cistern's dark and barely climbs back out. POV: Marguerite. Beat: trauma; the past stops being abstract.

chapters.title: The Thing with Fingerprints
chapters.summary: It finally shows itself fully: Étienne and something older wearing him, the drowned boy fused with whatever the parents had summoned or become. It doesn't threaten her — it asks, politely, to be let out. POV: Marguerite. Beat: pity and revulsion in the same breath.

chapters.title: Camille Comes Home
chapters.summary: Marguerite brings Camille to the house against her doctor's advice. Crossing the threshold, Camille ages visibly, the house reclaiming its interest. She agrees to speak the truth aloud on the property. POV: alternating. Beat: duty and love reconciled — Camille returns for her brother, not her absolution.

chapters.title: The Confession at the Well
chapters.summary: At the sealed cistern, Camille names what her parents did and what she failed to do, while the frost closes over the last clear window. The house shakes; every mirror shows the 1974 kitchen at once. POV: alternating. Beat: climax — truth as exorcism.

chapters.title: Breaking the Seal
chapters.summary: Marguerite and Camille open the cistern together and carry Étienne's small remains into daylight, the first light to touch them in fifty years. The thing with fingerprints unravels into a boy-shaped absence, then nothing. POV: Marguerite. Beat: release, grief, awe.

chapters.title: One Second Early
chapters.summary: The mirrors now reflect a half-second ahead — showing Marguerite safe acts before she performs them. The frost recedes. But one mirror shows a figure standing behind her that isn't there when she turns. POV: Marguerite. Beat: peace undercut by residue.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Keeps
chapters.summary: She buries Étienne beside his grandmother under a plum tree, keeps one fingerprint cast as evidence of nothing and everything, and quits pest control — or thinks she does. Camille, freed, remembers her brother laughing. POV: Marguerite. Beat: mourning transformed into custodianship.

chapters.title: The Next Call
chapters.summary: Months later, a new client calls about a house where the mirrors run late. Marguerite says yes before she can stop herself, packing her kit and Étienne's cast. In her rearview mirror, her reflection smiles a half-second early. POV: Marguerite. Beat: resolution as continuation — some debts must be collected forever.
